planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; give plants generous spacing and good airflow to reduce leaf-spot pressure.

directions: Japanese photinia is the smaller-growing, glossier-leaved parent species behind the popular Photinia x fraseri hybrid, forming a dense, rounded evergreen shrub with elliptical, deep-green leaves that flush copper-bronze rather than the brilliant scarlet of its hybrid offspring. Small white flower clusters open in mid-spring with a somewhat strong scent, followed by red berries that persist into winter and draw songbirds. It tolerates shearing into a formal hedge or screen but keeps a more naturally tidy shape than P. x fraseri if left alone, and it is somewhat less prone to Entomosporium leaf spot when given full sun and open spacing. Provide well-drained, slightly acidic soil and avoid overhead irrigation, which spreads fungal leaf-spot spores between plants.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with wide spacing; the large leaves and vigorous habit need extra room compared to standard Red Tip Photinia to keep air moving through the canopy.

directions: Robusta is an older, larger-leaved, more vigorous selection of Photinia x fraseri than the common Red Tip cultivar, producing broader, thicker, more leathery foliage and a coarser, bolder texture that many growers find shows leaf-spot damage less conspicuously than finer-leaved forms. New growth still emerges in the characteristic bronze-red flush, though somewhat less brilliant scarlet than Red Tip, maturing to a deep, glossy green. Because it grows larger and coarser than standard Red Tip, Robusta suits tall screens and large-scale plantings better than tight foundation hedges. Give it full sun, good drainage, and generous spacing to minimize the Entomosporium leaf spot that plagues crowded, shaded plantings of this hybrid.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Birmingham's more upright habit lends itself well to tall privacy screens as well as sheared hedges.

directions: Birmingham is an old, vigorous, upright-growing selection of Photinia x fraseri long favored in southern nurseries for its faster growth and taller ultimate size compared to the compact Red Tip cultivar, making it a popular choice for quick, tall privacy screens along property lines. It produces the same brilliant red new-growth flush as other Fraser photinia selections, followed by white spring flower clusters and red-brown berries, with foliage maturing to glossy dark green. Like all Photinia x fraseri selections, Birmingham is vulnerable to Entomosporium leaf spot in humid, crowded conditions with poor air circulation, so plant with generous spacing in full sun and avoid wetting the foliage with sprinklers. Periodic shearing controls size and encourages the colorful new growth flush, though heavy shearing also increases disease-susceptible tender tissue.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this very dwarf, mounding selection needs minimal spacing compared to the species and fits low borders and small foundation beds.

directions: Pringles Dwarf is a very slow-growing, low-mounding selection of yew podocarpus that stays well under three feet tall even after many years, forming a dense cushion of the same narrow, flat, dark-green, yew-like leaves found on the full-size species. It fills the role of a fine-textured, low evergreen border or foundation plant in situations where standard or even Compacta podocarpus would eventually outgrow the space. Like all podocarpus, it tolerates shade, clay soil, salt spray, and drought far better than most needled evergreens and needs only light shaping, if any, to hold its naturally neat, rounded form. It is essentially untroubled by pests or disease in Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: Florida Nursery, Growers and Landscape Association

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing tightly for a dense, narrow screen; this columnar form needs less lateral room than the species.

directions: Angustifolius is a narrow-leaved, tightly columnar selection of yew podocarpus prized for screening in tight side yards and narrow property-line plantings where a full-spreading podocarpus would be too wide. Its needle-like leaves are noticeably slimmer than the species, packed densely along upright branches to create a slender, formal silhouette that still tolerates shearing if an even tighter hedge form is wanted. Like other podocarpus selections, it handles shade, clay soil, salt spray, and drought far better than most conifers, grows slowly, and remains largely free of pest and disease problems in Gulf Coast landscapes. Its narrow habit makes it a useful alternative to Italian cypress in humid climates where cypress often struggles with fungal blight.
sources: Florida Nursery, Growers and Landscape Association
